## Core Overview
- **Primary Purpose:** Introduce the Divide and Conquer design strategy for algorithms by breaking problems into multiple smaller subproblems, solving them recursively, and combining the results.
- **Fundamental Themes:** Contrast with Decrease and Conquer, analyze sorting algorithms (Merge Sort and Quick Sort), and master recurrence relations using the Master Theorem.

## Key Concepts & Theorems/Formulas
- **Divide and Conquer Core Idea:**
  - Split -> Solve -> Combine
  - Base case: solve very small instances directly.
- **Recurrence Relations:**
  - General form: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
  - a = number of recursive subproblems
  - b = shrink factor for each subproblem
  - f(n) = work done outside recursive calls (divide and combine steps)
- **Merge Sort:**
  - Strategy: Divide array into fixed halves, recursively sort, and merge.
  - Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)
  - Time Complexity: O(n log n) for Best, Average, and Worst cases.
  - Space Complexity: O(n) auxiliary memory.
  - Property: Stable sorting algorithm.
- **Quick Sort:**
  - Strategy: Choose a pivot, partition array by value so elements <= pivot are left and > pivot are right, then recurse.
  - Best/Average Time: O(n log n)
  - Worst Time: O(n^2) when partitions are highly unbalanced (e.g., T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)).
  - Space Complexity: O(log n) stack space, in-place partitioning.
  - Property: Typically unstable.
- **Maximum Subarray Problem:**
  - Solved via Divide and Conquer by checking left half, right half, and crossing midpoint.
  - Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) -> O(n log n).

## Exam Takeaways
- **Merge Sort vs Quick Sort:** Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time and stability at the cost of O(n) extra space. Quick Sort offers in-place sorting and superior average performance, but suffers an O(n^2) worst-case with poor pivot selection.
- **Recurrence Justification:** Always tie each term in a recurrence relation (like O(n) merge work) back to actual algorithmic operations.
- **Partitioning Rule:** Quick Sort partitioning places the pivot into its final sorted position; the pivot is excluded from subsequent recursive calls.
